newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russia cools heated precious metal markets.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russia cools heated precious metal markets.

text.p: Russia moved to calm jittery precious metals markets on Tuesday by assuring customers that delayed 1997 exports of platinum and palladium would begin soon.

Prices of the rare metals slid in response to a statement released by the export agent for platinum group metals (PGM), Almazjuvelirexport (Almaz), although traders were still cautious after experiencing so many false dawns already this year.
"You are bound to get some kind of knee-jerk reaction to this kind of news," said Rhona O'Connell, metals markets analyst at T. Hoare and Co in London.
Spot palladium prices in London dropped $6.25 an ounce to around $167.75 after the announcement. Platinum also tracked sharply lower, losing $9.50 to about $387.25.
Almaz said talks with Japan had already started, and that deliveries should begin by mid-June. It also said that there was enough palladium around to fulfil customers' 1997 needs.

Palladium prices raced to a two-year high on Monday, partly on continuing delays in exports from Russia, the world's number one palladium supplier and number two platinum producer, to Japan, which is the world's biggest consumer of both.
Platinum has also risen on the export snags, although Russia is less dominant in the platinum supply table.

Almaz PGM department director Vitaly Berlin, who signed the statement, was not immediately available for comment. But traders and analysts said the announcement appeared to be aimed at calming the platinum and palladium markets.
The agency even said it could deliver enough metal to world markets "to keep palladium prices at a reasonable level".
"My guess would be that this is around about $160," O'Connell said.
Traders in London said that an element of doubt would remain until Russian supplies actually started to flow, but the news pointed to a return to more normal market conditions.

"The market will come lower because everybody has been long as it was too risky to be short," said one. "I would think you should be looking for opportunities to sell and probably start lending the metal."
The cost of borrowing as well as buying the metal outright rose sharply in recent weeks in reaction to supply tightness.
Analysts said the threat of substitution triggered by high palladium prices may have explained why Almaz moved to dampen sentiment when it did, rather than riding prices even higher.
Some see $200 an ounce as a realistic medium-term target if Russian delays continue.
Palladium's main end-use is electronic components, and Japanese industry sources said earlier on Tuesday that they were stepping up efforts to switch to cheaper materials such as nickel.
The reasons for such long delays in exports of the lucrative hard currency earners remain a mystery to the outside world.
Some Western traders speculated that a behind-the-scenes struggle for control of Russia's PGM exports between Almaz and the central bank was one factor holding up the talks.
The growing importance of the central bank and commercial operations in Russia's newly-liberalised gold market only served to fuel the rumours.
Others said that after emptying its stores of precious metals in recent years, Russia needed to replenish reserves.
Russian officials played down the rumours all along, saying instead that a cabinet shake-up and delays in passing the 1997 federal budget were the main factors.
